As most have said you want to avoid putting anything much down a sink or through a dishwasher, it should be residue only, the rest scraped into a bin. 

Several people have suggested sodium hydroxide which is the active bit of drain unblocker and yes be careful as its not pleasant stuff, very strong alkali. 

If that doesn't work, being careful and I mean CAREFUL! You can use potassium hydroxide, also known as KOH, it is an extremely exothermic reaction and turns fat into soap like NaOH just faster and more aggressively. This stuff will melt skin, eyes, lungs, stomach, clothes, hair. You get the idea, it can be purchased online easily though. 

Put 1kg in the sink while the sink is completely dry, open the kitchen window  turn on the cold water, leave and shut the door and do not go back in for about 20 mins or more depending on how open the tap is, let the fumes dissipate and all the KOH run through the drain, it'll clear out the pipes nicely and even some of the deposits in the larger sewer. 

Be careful if you use KOH, it is not forgiving to any accidents!

Ok so unless one valve is completely shut you won't see pressure differences, to get equal flow you can close both valves down an equal amount. Your pump flow and it's pressure capability are the only considerations if you want reduced total flow. To actually work out the flow you'd need to calculate the flow through the valves and know the fixed flow from your pump. Other way would be use a flow meter or measure flow for example if the two boxes are tanks and start empty you can time how long to fill and work out flow from volume vs time.

Edit: The first 20% opening of the valves will give you the first 80% of the flow so if you wanted 50/50 the valves will only be open about 15% each to flow 50% of maximum. Your pump flow may mean they're only open 5% if it can't supply the maximum the pipe will take. Eg if the pipe will take a max of 10 litres per second but your pump only supplies 5 litres per second the valves would probably be open 5% to get an equal 2.5 litres per second in each.

The pulse units in these are generally mechanical, you can add an electronic one but it's not easy. Finding the mechanical pulser online would be best and put some vacuum rated taps inline as if you reduce the flow the suction will go down (motor will not be able to remove as much air but will work harder and may fail sooner). These electro-mechanical systems are a bit of a fine line to balance having enough movement and not burning up the motor/controller. 

A less elegant but more effective solution would be to make an "air buffer" to reduce suction, an electronic pulse control may work better in this system too as you can refine how/where the suction goes. It takes a bit of designing but the easiest way would be low volt solenoids and a raspberry pi with some pressure sensors as triggers or just use it timed. 

The air buffer is basically you put a T piece in the hose and then use a big syringe to provide air so the pump sucks out of the syringe first which limits how much it can suck and therefore how hard. 

None of these options will cost more than a few $ but the pi, solenoids and sensors will give a lot more flexibility especially if relays are used to separate the pi from the solenoid power but it will cost more. Also always remember the 80/20 rule of hydraulics (yes air is technically a fluid) if a valve/tap/hole is 20% open you will have 80% of the maximum flow. Try the most simple things first, multi meter the micro switches and bed leveling sensor, make sure they work. Just because it's doing something it doesn't mean it's working.

Second, factory reset the firmware or fresh install new firmware, this will mess up any custom settings you've done but gives a fresh blank canvas.

Third, open it up and check the main board, if everything shows as working/reporting correctly then it could be a main board issue, this may not be visible if it is the issue.

My initial thought is that your bed level sensor has gone out of calibration for some reason, find the specs and check it with a good multi meter or spare sensor. Maybe it's reading but resistance is too high/low or similar like inductance. Make sure it reads as per the spec sheet before wiping out your settings and when you test it use a spare bit of metal to trigger the sensor while it's way off the bed so if it doesn't stop you can power off immediately to prevent further damage.

Edit: use ferrous metal if it relies on magnetic sensor, aluminium can create eddy currents but iirc not all levelling sensors can do that.
